title: Did We Find Them All?
coreInsight: A difficult universe can be partitioned into cases that are exhaustive, non-overlapping, and easier to count.
targetLearnerRealization: Good casework partitions every possibility exactly once into categories that are easier to count.
learningObjectives: Recognize when an unstructured list does not prove completeness.
Choose a case variable that creates exhaustive, non-overlapping groups.
Count within manageable cases and combine their totals.

continuity.openingCallback: You already know how to make a systematic list. Now we will ask what makes that list trustworthy.
closingSeeds: A clean case split can become cumbersome when natural cases overlap.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: A few natural cases are automatically exhaustive.
Cases are useful even when each is as difficult as the original problem.
The best case split need not reflect the problem's actual constraint.

beats.purpose: Give the learner a small space where informal listing feels plausible before structure is imposed.
beats.expectedRealization: Several sequences work, but finding a count is not the same as proving completeness.
beats.transitionIn: In systematic listing, organization helped you keep track. First, try this one without any suggested categories.
beats.transitionOut: You found a count. Now ask the harder question: why should anyone trust that the list is complete?
beats.whyNow: A four-outcome movement puzzle makes it easy to start listing and hard to justify stopping without a structure.
beats.entryBridge: Write the sequences in whatever order they occur to you. Do not sort them yet.
beats.exitBridge: Four is the right count, but the number alone does not prove that nothing was missed or counted twice.
learnerPrompts: List each sequence before entering the total.

beats.purpose: Reveal the complete outcome set in an intentionally unstructured order so completeness still feels uncertain.
beats.expectedRealization: Seeing four plausible outcomes still does not explain why there cannot be another.
beats.transitionIn: Here are the four sequences we found, left in discovery order.
beats.caption: A list can look finished without proving that it is finished.

beats.purpose: Turn completeness into a genuine learner question before offering the organizing method.
beats.expectedRealization: A convincing count needs a reason every possibility appears exactly once.
beats.prompt: Are these all of them? What would prove that we did not miss a sequence or count one twice?

response.rubric: The learner should seek a systematic organization or another completeness argument.
response.revealAfterSubmit: A longer list is not yet a proof. We need a structure that gives every valid sequence exactly one place to go.

beats.purpose: Let the learner create exhaustive, non-overlapping cases by assigning every outcome to one move-count bucket.
beats.expectedRealization: Number of moves gives each sequence one and only one bucket, and each bucket is easy to finish.
beats.transitionIn: Sort every card by one feature that each sequence has exactly once: its number of moves.
beats.prompt: Put each sequence into its move-count case.

response.feedback: The buckets contain 1, 2, and 1 sequences. Every card has exactly one home.

beats.correctFeedback: Every sequence has exactly one move count, so the cases cannot overlap. Because positive moves totaling 3 use 1, 2, or 3 moves, the cases also cover everything.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count the addends on each card. A card belongs in exactly one move-count bucket.

beats.purpose: Extract the three properties the learner's organization just demonstrated.
beats.expectedRealization: Useful cases cover all outcomes, do not overlap, and simplify the remaining count.
beats.heading: What the bins proved
beats.body: They cover every possible move count. They never overlap. Inside each smaller bin, we can finish the list systematically.

beats.purpose: Name the structure only after the learner has built and justified it.
beats.expectedRealization: Casework is the name for the organizing move already used.
beats.transitionIn: You have already used the technique. Now give it a name.
beats.name: Casework
beats.conciseDefinition: Split all possibilities into exhaustive, non-overlapping cases that are each easier to count.

beats.purpose: Shift attention from executing casework to choosing a split that follows the problem's constraint.
beats.expectedRealization: The best case variable often comes directly from the strongest restriction.
beats.transitionIn: The hardest part is often not counting the cases. It is choosing the right case headers.
beats.transitionOut: Keep those position-based case headers. We are about to swap in a different digit condition.
beats.prompt: Using 1, 2, 3, and 4 without repetition, we want to count three-digit even numbers. Which first split makes the remaining work cleanest?

options.text: Split by whether the ones digit is 2 or 4
Split into numbers below or above 300

feedback.hundreds: The hundreds digit does not decide whether the number is even.
feedback.tens: The tens digit does not carry the even-number restriction.
feedback.ones: Exactly. Every even number ends in either 2 or 4, never both.
feedback.size: That split is possible, but it does not simplify the even-number condition.

beats.correctFeedback: The ones digit is the useful case variable because the condition itself restricts that position.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Look for the position that determines whether the whole number is even.

beats.purpose: Carry the position-bin representation into the bank problem and let the learner choose its case headers before seeing the solution animation.
beats.expectedRealization: Exactly one zero can be classified by its legal position, giving two labeled, disjoint bins.
beats.prompt: Now make zero the special digit. For a three-digit number with exactly one zero, which case headers keep the organizer complete and non-overlapping?

visual.ariaLabel: Two cases classified by the restricted digit position

options.text: Zero in hundreds, tens, or ones
Zero in tens or zero in ones

feedback.all-positions: A zero in the hundreds place would not produce a three-digit number.
feedback.legal-positions: Exactly. The one zero must be in one of these two positions, never both.
feedback.number-size: Those bins cover the numbers, but they do not simplify the zero condition.
feedback.digit-types: Those labels classify digits, not the three-digit outcomes we need to count.

beats.correctFeedback: Keep two bins: zero in tens and zero in ones. Every valid number belongs to exactly one.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use the zero's legal position, and remember that the leading digit cannot be zero.

beats.purpose: Apply the learner's case-quality tests to the approved authentic problem while preserving the position-bin representation.
beats.expectedRealization: Exactly one zero creates two exhaustive and non-overlapping position cases, each with a simple product count.
beats.transitionIn: Keep the same two-bin organizer, but let the special digit be zero.
beats.transitionOut: The exact-one condition made the bins clean. Changing that condition will test how well this strategy scales.
beats.whyNow: Exactly one zero in a three-digit number splits naturally by the zero's position, making the case partition concrete and checkable.
beats.entryBridge: After the lesson's 1/2/3-move warmup, keep the case headers visible and replace them with 'zero in tens' and 'zero in ones'.
beats.exitBridge: Immediately mutate the condition from exactly one zero to at least one zero so the clean case split starts to strain, launching C5.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Outcome cards that physically sort into labeled, non-overlapping bins.
learnerPrompts: What feature could every valid number be classified by?
Could any valid number land in both cases?
Could any valid number land in neither?

beats.purpose: Harvest the general method from the bank problem instead of ending on its numerical answer.
beats.expectedRealization: The success came from the partition, not from an isolated digit trick.
beats.heading: The answer was not the main prize
beats.body: The zero's position forced two complete, separate cases. Each case reduced to two independent choices, so 81 + 81 counted every valid number once.
beats.transitionOut: Now use the same three tests without guidance: complete, separate, manageable.

beats.purpose: Clearly end the teaching narrative and begin independent evidence.
beats.heading: Independent practice
beats.body: For each problem, choose the case headers before doing the arithmetic. Ask whether every outcome appears exactly once.

beats.purpose: Check a direct transfer in which parity supplies two clean cases.
beats.expectedRealization: Even sums split into odd-odd and even-even cases.
beats.whyNow: This checks whether the learner can construct exhaustive cases from a familiar condition without copying the movement example.
beats.entryBridge: Let the sum condition choose the cases.
beats.exitBridge: Odd-odd and even-even are exhaustive and cannot overlap, giving 4 + 4 = 8 codes.
learnerPrompts: Which parity pairings make an even sum?

beats.purpose: Check systematic case completion when case sizes decrease.
beats.expectedRealization: Fixing the left card makes the legal right-card choices easy to exhaust.
beats.whyNow: The cases are unequal, so the learner must count inside each rather than multiply one repeated case size.
beats.entryBridge: Choose one position to fix, then finish each smaller count.
beats.exitBridge: Fixing the left card gives case sizes 4, 3, 2, 1, and 0, totaling 10.
learnerPrompts: If the left card is fixed, how many larger right cards remain?

beats.purpose: Mix casework with a constrained distribution representation.
beats.expectedRealization: Fixing one labeled box's count turns the remaining distribution into a short list.
beats.whyNow: This changes surface context and representation while preserving the need for exhaustive, disjoint cases.
beats.entryBridge: Find a quantity whose possible values create a short, complete set of cases.
beats.exitBridge: Box A can hold 1, 2, or 3 counters; those cases contribute 3, 2, and 1 distributions, totaling 6.
learnerPrompts: What values can Box A have while leaving at least one counter for each other box?

beats.purpose: Mix casework with translating a perimeter condition and removing rotational duplicates.
beats.expectedRealization: Ordering the shorter side creates a complete, non-duplicated dimension list.
beats.whyNow: The learner must choose a convention that prevents the same rectangle from entering two cases.
beats.entryBridge: Build the cases so a rotated rectangle cannot be counted twice.
beats.exitBridge: Taking the shorter side as 1, 2, 3, or 4 gives four distinct rectangles and prevents reversals from duplicating them.
learnerPrompts: How can you order the side lengths so each rectangle appears once?

beats.purpose: Check authentic transfer where the learner must identify the terminal digit as the useful case variable.
beats.expectedRealization: The multiple-of-5 condition creates the exhaustive final-digit cases 0 and 5, with different counts inside them.
beats.whyNow: The problem disguises casework among several digit restrictions and requires the learner to choose the split independently.
beats.entryBridge: One condition in this problem offers exactly two useful case headers. Find it before counting.
beats.exitBridge: A multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5. Those disjoint cases contribute 36 and 48 numbers, for 84 total.
learnerPrompts: Write the case headers before calculating; then check that they cover every multiple of 5.

beats.purpose: Seed the limitation that motivates complementary counting without teaching the next technique.
beats.expectedRealization: Casework is strongest when its cases stay clean; overlapping conditions can make the split cumbersome.
beats.transitionIn: One last stress test for the organizer you built.
beats.prompt: Exactly one zero gave each number one case. If the condition became at least one zero, would 'zero in tens' and 'zero in ones' still be non-overlapping?
beats.takeaway: No. A number such as 100 belongs to both descriptions. Casework still works in principle, but the bookkeeping is getting ugly. What might we do when the opposite set is cleaner?

notes: Manually authored gold benchmark; no automated lesson generation was used.
The generated teaching problem was preferred because it creates the completeness question more cleanly than the mapped bank problem.
The fixed authentic final transfer is amc8-2011-23.
